Maglemosian (c. 9000 – c. 6000 BC) is the name given to a [culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeological_culture) of the early [Mesolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesolithic) period in [Northern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Europe). In [Scandinavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavia), the culture was succeeded by the [Kongemose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kongemose_culture) culture.
The name originates from the [Danish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark) archeological site Maglemose, situated near [Gørlev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gørlev) and [Høng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Høng) on western [Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealand_(Denmark)), southwest of lake [Tissø](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tissø). Here the first settlement of the culture was excavated in 1900, by George Sarauw.[[1]](./Maglemosian_culture#cite_note-1) During the following century a long series of similar settlements were excavated from [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England) to [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland) and from [Skåne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skåne) in [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden) to northern [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France).
When the Maglemosian culture flourished, sea levels were much lower than now and what is now mainland Europe and Scandinavia were linked with Britain. The cultural period overlaps the end of the [last ice age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weichselian_glaciation),[[2]](./Maglemosian_culture#cite_note-2) when the ice retreated and the glaciers melted. It was a long process and sea levels in [Northern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Europe) did not reach current levels until almost 6000 BC, by which time they had inundated large territories previously inhabited by Maglemosian people. Therefore, there is hope that the emerging discipline of [underwater archaeology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_archaeology) may reveal interesting findings related to the Maglemosian culture in the future.
The Maglemosian people lived in forest and wetland environments, using fishing and hunting tools made from wood, bone, and flint [microliths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microlith). It appears that they had domesticated the [dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dog).[[3]](./Maglemosian_culture#cite_note-3) Some may have lived settled lives, but most were nomadic.[[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed)]
Huts made of bark have been preserved, in addition to tools made of [flint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flint), [bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone), and [horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horn_(anatomy)). A characteristic feature of the culture is the sharply edged [microliths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microlith) of flintstone, used for spear and arrow heads.[[4]](./Maglemosian_culture#cite_note-4) Another notable feature is the [leister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leister), a characteristic type of fishing spear, used for [gigging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigging).

content.text:
This Wikipedia page is about the **Maglemosian culture**, which was an early Mesolithic (Middle Stone Age) culture that existed in Northern Europe from approximately 9000 to 6000 BC.

Here are the key points about what the page covers:

**Geographic and Temporal Context:**
- The culture stretched across Northern Europe from England to Poland and from southern Sweden to northern France
- It flourished during a time when sea levels were much lower, and Britain was connected to mainland Europe
- The period overlapped with the end of the last ice age

**Discovery and Naming:**
- Named after the Danish archaeological site Maglemose near Gørlev and Høng in western Zealand
- First excavated in 1900 by George Sarauw

**Lifestyle and Technology:**
- The Maglemosian people lived in forest and wetland environments
- They were primarily hunter-gatherers who used fishing and hunting tools
- They had domesticated dogs
- Most were nomadic, though some may have lived more settled lives
- They built huts made of bark

**Material Culture:**
- Made tools from wood, bone, flint, and horn
- Known for their characteristic sharply edged flint microliths used for spear and arrow heads
- Used a distinctive type of fishing spear called a "leister"

**Archaeological Significance:**
- The culture was succeeded by the Kongemose culture in Scandinavia
- Many Maglemosian sites may now be underwater due to rising sea levels, making underwater archaeology potentially valuable for future discoveries

The page provides both historical context about this important prehistoric culture and details about their material remains and way of life.

This script calculates Fibonacci numbers and exports results to an Excel file.

import pandas as pd
import os

def fibonacci(n):
    """
    Calculate the nth Fibonacci number using iterative approach.
    
    Args:
        n (int): The position in the Fibonacci sequence (0-indexed)
        
    Returns:
        int: The nth Fibonacci number
    """
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("n must be a non-negative integer")
    elif n == 0:
        return 0
    elif n == 1:
        return 1
    
    # Iterative approach for efficiency
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(2, n + 1):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return b


def fibonacci_recursive(n):
    """
    Calculate the nth Fibonacci number using recursive approach.
    (Less efficient but more intuitive)
    
    Args:
        n (int): The position in the Fibonacci sequence (0-indexed)
        
    Returns:
        int: The nth Fibonacci number
    """
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("n must be a non-negative integer")
    elif n == 0:
        return 0
    elif n == 1:
        return 1
    else:
        return fibonacci_recursive(n - 1) + fibonacci_recursive(n - 2)


def generate_fibonacci_sequence(count):
    """
    Generate a sequence of Fibonacci numbers.
    
    Args:
        count (int): Number of Fibonacci numbers to generate
        
    Returns:
        list: List of tuples (position, fibonacci_number)
    """
    sequence = []
    for i in range(count):
        fib_num = fibonacci(i)
        sequence.append((i, fib_num))
    return sequence

        # Get the workbook and worksheet
        workbook = writer.book
        worksheet = writer.sheets['Fibonacci Sequence']
        
        # Add some formatting

        for cell in worksheet[1]:
            cell.font = Font(bold=True, size=12)
            cell.fill = PatternFill(start_color="4472C4", end_color="4472C4", fill_type="solid")
            cell.font = Font(bold=True, color="FFFFFF", size=12)
            cell.alignment = Alignment(horizontal='center')
        
        # Highlight the target row if specified

            target_row = target_n + 2  # +2 because of 1-indexing and header row
            for cell in worksheet[target_row]:
                cell.fill = PatternFill(start_color="FFFF00", end_color="FFFF00", fill_type="solid")
                cell.font = Font(bold=True)
        
        # Adjust column widths
        worksheet.column_dimensions['A'].width = 18

        # Add a summary section

        worksheet.cell(row=summary_row, column=1, value="Summary:")

## Design Outline

### Goals
1. Fixed-size pool of N goroutines processing jobs concurrently.
2. Submit work without blocking the producer (bounded queue with backpressure).
3. **Graceful shutdown**: stop accepting new jobs, finish in-flight work, return cleanly.
4. **Forced shutdown**: cancel in-flight work via `context.Context` if deadline exceeded.
5. Safe against double-close, double-submit-after-close, and worker panics.

### Components
| Component | Role |
|-----------|------|
| `Pool` | Public type holding workers, channels, context, and state. |
| `Job` | Interface (or func) representing a unit of work. Receives a `ctx`. |
| `jobs chan Job` | Bounded channel for backpressure. |
| `results chan Result` | Optional results stream. |
| `ctx, cancel` | For propagating cancellation to in-flight jobs. |
| `wg sync.WaitGroup` | Tracks active workers for clean Stop. |
| `closed atomic.Bool` | Guards against Submit-after-Stop and double-Stop. |

### Lifecycle
```
New(n, queueSize) → Start workers → Submit(jobs) ... → Stop(ctx)
                                                         │
                          ┌──────────────────────────────┤
                          ▼                              ▼
              close(jobs) → workers drain        ctx deadline → cancel() → workers exit
```

### Shutdown protocol (the tricky part)
1. `Stop(ctx)` flips `closed` so further `Submit` calls return an error.
2. Close the `jobs` channel → workers exit their `range` loop after draining queued work.
3. Wait on `wg` in a goroutine; race against the caller's `ctx`.
4. If `ctx` fires first, call `cancel()` so in-flight jobs see `ctx.Done()` and can abort.
5. Always wait for `wg` so no goroutine leaks (even after forced cancel).

### Invariants
- No send on closed `jobs` channel: gated by `closed` + a `sync.Mutex` around the send.
- No goroutine leaks: every started worker is in `wg`; `Stop` always `wg.Wait()`s.

package workerpool

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"sync"
	"sync/atomic"
)

// Job is a unit of work. The ctx is cancelled on forced shutdown.
type Job func(ctx context.Context) Result

// Result carries a job's output and/or error.
type Result struct {
	Value any
	Err   error
}

var (
	ErrPoolClosed = errors.New("worker pool: closed")
	ErrQueueFull  = errors.New("worker pool: queue full")
)

// Pool is a fixed-size worker pool.
type Pool struct {
	jobs    chan Job
	results chan Result

	ctx    context.Context
	cancel context.CancelFunc

	wg     sync.WaitGroup
	mu     sync.Mutex // guards sends on jobs against close
	closed atomic.Bool
}

// New creates and starts a pool with `workers` goroutines and a queue of size `queueSize`.
func New(workers, queueSize int) *Pool {
	if workers <= 0 {
		workers = 1
	}
	if queueSize < 0 {
		queueSize = 0
	}
	ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
	p := &Pool{
		jobs:    make(chan Job, queueSize),
		results: make(chan Result, queueSize),
		ctx:     ctx,
		cancel:  cancel,
	}
	p.wg.Add(workers)
	for i := 0; i < workers; i++ {
		go p.worker(i)
	}
	return p
}

func (p *Pool) worker(id int) {
	defer p.wg.Done()
	for job := range p.jobs { // exits when jobs is closed AND drained
		p.run(job)
	}
}

func (p *Pool) run(job Job) {
	defer func() {
		if r := recover(); r != nil {
			p.results <- Result{Err: fmt.Errorf("panic: %v", r)}
		}
	}()
	// Short-circuit if we've been force-cancelled.
	if err := p.ctx.Err(); err != nil {
		p.results <- Result{Err: err}
		return
	}
	p.results <- job(p.ctx)
}

// Submit enqueues a job. Returns an error if the pool is closed or the queue is full.
// Use SubmitBlocking for backpressure.
func (p *Pool) Submit(job Job) error {
	p.mu.Lock()
	defer p.mu.Unlock()
	if p.closed.Load() {
		return ErrPoolClosed
	}
	select {
	case p.jobs <- job:
		return nil
	default:
		return ErrQueueFull
	}
}

// SubmitBlocking blocks until the job is enqueued, the pool closes, or ctx is done.
func (p *Pool) SubmitBlocking(ctx context.Context, job Job) error {
	p.mu.Lock()
	if p.closed.Load() {
		p.mu.Unlock()
		return ErrPoolClosed
	}
	// Hold the mutex only across the non-blocking attempt; release before potentially blocking.
	select {
	case p.jobs <- job:
		p.mu.Unlock()
		return nil
	default:
	}
	p.mu.Unlock()

	select {
	case <-ctx.Done():
		return ctx.Err()
	case <-p.ctx.Done():
		return ErrPoolClosed
	default:
	}

	// Re-acquire to safely send; the channel might close concurrently with Stop.
	p.mu.Lock()
	defer p.mu.Unlock()
	if p.closed.Load() {
		return ErrPoolClosed
	}
	select {
	case p.jobs <- job:
		return nil
	case <-ctx.Done():
		return ctx.Err()
	}
}

// Results returns the channel jobs publish to. It is closed after Stop completes.
func (p *Pool) Results() <-chan Result { return p.results }

// Stop performs a graceful shutdown:
//   - Refuses new submissions immediately.
//   - Allows queued jobs to complete.
//   - If shutdownCtx expires, cancels in-flight jobs.
//   - Always waits for all workers to exit (no leaks).
func (p *Pool) Stop(shutdownCtx context.Context) error {
	// Make Stop idempotent.
	if !p.closed.CompareAndSwap(false, true) {
		return ErrPoolClosed
	}

	// Close jobs under the mutex so no Submit sends on a closed channel.
	p.mu.Lock()
	close(p.jobs)
	p.mu.Unlock()

	done := make(chan struct{})
	go func() {
		p.wg.Wait()
		close(done)
	}()

	var err error
	select {
	case <-done:
		// Graceful: all queued jobs finished.
	case <-shutdownCtx.Done():
		// Forced: cancel in-flight jobs, then still wait for workers to return.
		p.cancel()
		<-done
		err = shutdownCtx.Err()
	}

	p.cancel()         // release context resources
	close(p.results)   // safe: all workers have exited
	return err
}
